lesson.title: Students Take the Lead: The Founding of SNCC
lesson.summary: In April 1960, veteran organizer Ella Baker convened student activists from across the South to form the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, a deliberately grassroots, youth led organization distinct from the church based, minister led SCLC.
lesson.body:
By early 1960, a new form of civil rights protest was spreading rapidly across the South: college and high school students staging sit ins at segregated lunch counters, drawing national attention and putting economic pressure on stores that refused to serve them. As this wave of youth activism grew, Ella Baker, a veteran organizer who had spent decades in civil rights work, including serving as SCLC's executive director, saw an opportunity and a risk. She believed strongly that this new generation of student activists needed its own independent organization rather than being folded into SCLC or another existing group as a junior wing.

In April 1960, Baker convened a meeting of student activists at Shaw University in Raleigh, North Carolina, her own alma mater, bringing together participants from sit in campaigns across the South. Out of that meeting came the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, usually known by its initials, SNCC, pronounced snick. Marion Barry, a graduate student who would later become mayor of Washington, D.C., served as SNCC's first chairman, and early leaders and members included Diane Nash and John Lewis, both of whom had been central to the Nashville sit in campaign.

Baker's influence shaped SNCC's structure from the start. Rather than build the kind of top down, minister led organization SCLC represented, Baker pushed for what she described as group centered leadership rather than a leader centered group, meaning that SNCC valued decentralized, local, grassroots organizing over dependence on a single charismatic figure. This was a real and lasting distinction between the two organizations. SCLC operated through networks of affiliated Black churches led largely by adult ministers, King prominent among them, while SNCC organized through students and young field workers who often lived for months at a time in small, dangerous rural communities to build local leadership from the ground up, particularly around voter registration.

SNCC worked alongside SCLC and older organizations like the NAACP through the early 1960s, and its members would go on to play central roles in the sit in movement's continued growth and the 1961 Freedom Rides. Over the course of the decade, SNCC's outlook shifted considerably: the organization that began committed to interracial cooperation and strict nonviolence grew more skeptical of both as its young organizers faced sustained, often lethal violence with little protection from federal authorities, a shift that became most visible later in the 1960s under leaders like Stokely Carmichael, who took over as chairman in 1966 and helped popularize the philosophy of Black Power, marking SNCC's evolution toward a more radical stance than its founding vision.
